title: Proposal: `optionDeleted` event for <datalist> and tags with valid @list

labels.name: needs implementer interest
labels.description: Moving the issue forward requires implementers to express interest

body:
### Introductory paragraph

I propose adding a new DOM event I'll temporarily call `optionDeleted`.

# Current situation
## Current example good behavior

Deleting proposed input options is not something new.
If you use autofill attribute [`autocomplete`](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-control-infrastructure.html#autofill) not set to `off`, the browser will store the multiple information inserted for later use (E.g. firefox can be set to always store if not set to `off`).

### The behavior with `autocomplete` + `Del` key
When the user selects an option using the keyboard or the mouse (not clicking in the mouse's case), the user has the option to remove that specific option by pressing the `Del` key (or any correspondent in locals I don't know).

## Current example bad behavior
Although the UI has the same basic appearance of what I specified above, that behavior is inconsistent with what happens if you use of `<datalist>` through the `@list` attribute.

### Here's why I believe it's bad
In both chrome and firefox, if you try to apply the above-mention procedure to delete an entry, that entry disappears but it is later on reloaded into the input upon any change.
Here's an example with firefox:
![deletingDatalistOptions](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/639467/82141674-5e3a8600-982f-11ea-98b5-867f0dae6760.gif)
(page used for the example: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/datalist)

# ...And so I propose

`optionDeleted` event.

## What the event is

`optionDeleted` is an event announcing the user ordered the UA for the removal of the fill suggestion.

### Firing process

This new event is fired at the input location when the user instructs the UA to delete an option generated from a `datalist`.
In this example interaction, the event would have been fired when I deleted the option. Such as in this scenario, when I delete the "Chocolate` option.
![Deleting Chocolate](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/639467/82143019-a3af8100-9838-11ea-8cc3-ab1cd0e9c9a5.gif)

## Event composition
This new event:

1. Bubbles
2. Is cancelable (optional implementation)
3. Contains a new attribute `option`

#### Cancelation (optional implementation)
If the event is canceled, the entry in the user's UI is not removed when the user orders so.
It's up to the website's UX to provide user feedback if this event is canceled.

#### `option` attribute
The `option` attribute of the new `Event` interface contains the pointer to the `<datalist>` option the user ordered its removal from.

E.g. In this HTML excerpt:
```
<input list="ice-cream-flavors" id="ice-cream-choice" name="ice-cream-choice" />
<datalist id="ice-cream-flavors">
    <option value="Chocolate">
    <option value="Coconut">
</datalist>
```
If I do as exemplified here:
![Deleting Chocolate](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/639467/82143019-a3af8100-9838-11ea-8cc3-ab1cd0e9c9a5.gif)
For the new event interface,
- `target` will point to `<input list="ice-cream-flavors" id="ice-cream-choice" name="ice-cream-choice" />`
- `option` will point to `<option value="Chocolate">` (inside the `<datalist>`)

## Event example implementation
Along with it, I propose, as a possible process, to create a new interface for `optionDeleted`. 

In javascript, such event would be defined for example as (with `[Event params]` as a placeholder for the Event constructor parameters):

```
class OptionDeletedEvent extends Event {
    constructor([Event params], optionDeleted) {
        super([Event params]);
        this.__optionDeleted = optionDeleted;
    }
    get option() {
        return this.__optionDeleted;
    }
}
```

## In summary:

1. **Dispatched** at the `<input>` where the user instructed the option to be deleted at.
2. New Event interface to accommodate new attribute (`option`).
2. Optional cancelable implementation
3. Allow JS to identify when and that the user intents to remove options from a `<datalist>`.

# Notes:
1. Due to my system, I can only test on Firefox and Chromium.
2. Examples are taken from: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/datalist
